aliases: Су Чжоу Мо Ли Хуа Ча
processing: A reprocessed tea: finished tea is scented with fresh jasmine blossoms. As with other Chinese jasmine teas, the base is usually green and the scenting can be repeated for a stronger, cleaner aroma.
harvest_season: As is typical of jasmine tea, the base tea is usually picked in spring and scented later, when the jasmine flowers in summer.
appearance_dry: Typical of jasmine green teas, fine dark-green strands, sometimes with a few dried blossoms.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow-green and clear, as usual for jasmine on a green base.
appearance_wet: Soft green leaf, like other green-based jasmine teas.
taste_profile: A fresh, rich and mellow cup, with clear jasmine perfume over a soft green tea body.

brewing.notes: These are usual settings for green-based jasmine. Hotter water and longer steeps bring out bitterness from the base tea.

vintage_note: Jasmine tea is sold by grade and number of scentings more often than by year, and it is best drunk within a year or two while the aroma is lively. Little is documented about how Suzhou lots in particular are dated, so ask for the scenting year.
description:
Suzhou jasmine tea is a scented tea from one of China's older jasmine centres, usually counted among the famous teas of Jiangsu. Fuzhou is better known today, so the Suzhou name is one you will meet less often.

It is a reprocessed tea, made by bringing finished tea together with jasmine blossoms so the leaf takes up the perfume. Details specific to Suzhou are poorly documented. As with other Chinese jasmine, the number of scentings and the quality of the base tea decide much of the result.

Expect a fresh, full and mellow cup with jasmine at the front. Brew it as a green tea, with water below the boil and short steeps, because scalding brings out bitterness more quickly than it brings out flowers.

When buying, smell the dry leaf: natural scenting should smell like flowers, not like perfume. Ask what the base tea is and how many times it was scented, because a bare regional name tells you little.
history:
Suzhou is recorded as growing jasmine for use in tea in the Song dynasty, according to Chinese accounts of its famous teas. By 1860 Suzhou jasmine tea was reportedly selling widely in the northeast and north of China.

Little is documented about who shaped the local style or how production has changed since.
